vignette:
He is 24 and works as a pharmacist, a job he once thought would suit him because it asked for calm, precision, and a steady voice. Before the trauma, he describes himself as careful and a little quiet, someone who liked routines and knew how to keep his head down. He is single and has not been in a relationship for a while, though he used to imagine that would change once he felt more settled in his work and daily life. Now he says life feels divided into before and after.

The event centers on his younger brother, who is injured in a sudden accident that happens without warning and changes everything in a matter of minutes. He is not there when it begins, and that remains one of the hardest parts for him. He remembers the first call, then the second, and the way his body seemed to go cold before his mind could catch up. For days afterward, he moves through the world as if he is functioning by force of habit rather than choice. He goes to work because he does not know what else to do, stands behind the pharmacy counter, counts tablets, answers questions, and tries to look composed, but he says it feels as though part of him is still in the hospital corridor waiting for news.

In the early weeks, he cannot stop replaying the sequence of calls, wondering what he should have done differently, what he might have said faster, which road he should have taken, and whether he would have arrived in time if he had left earlier. He knows, rationally, that he was not responsible for what happened, but the knowledge does not quiet the guilt. At work, he becomes intensely alert to sound. A phone ringing too sharply, a sudden vibration in his pocket, or a colleague calling his name across the dispensary can jolt him into a wave of panic. He notices that his heart pounds, his hands tremble slightly when he is making up scripts, and he has to read labels twice because his attention slips away into images of the accident and the hospital.

Sleep becomes difficult. When he does sleep, he wakes suddenly, disoriented, with his chest tight and his mind already searching for bad news. Some nights he lies awake long after midnight, staring at the ceiling and thinking about the last ordinary conversation he had with his brother. He becomes wary of silence because it gives his mind room to return to that day. He also begins to avoid places that remind him of the trauma, including the hospital parking area and the route he took during those first frantic visits. Even seeing a similar car model to the one involved can bring a rush of dread. He says his body reacts before he has time to think.

He notices himself changing in ways that disturb him. He used to feel emotionally available to his family, but now he often feels numb, as if his feelings are sealed behind glass. His mother says he seems distant, and he does not argue because he can see that she is right. He has trouble talking about his brother without becoming overwhelmed, so he keeps conversations practical and brief. Friends invite him out, and he often declines, saying he is tired or working early the next day, though the deeper truth is that being around people feels effortful and strangely unreal. He finds himself scanning for danger, tense in crowded places, and irritated by small interruptions at work. Patients’ questions, once manageable, now sometimes feel like demands he can barely tolerate.

Over time, he tries to stay busy because stillness leaves too much room for memory. He takes extra shifts and stays late organizing stock, enjoying the simple order of pharmacy tasks because they let him focus on something concrete. Even so, he feels more fragile than he appears. Certain smells, the sound of a siren, or a message alert on his phone can pull him back into the same surge of fear and helplessness. He keeps going, but he describes it as an effort of discipline rather than confidence. He is still caring for others, still speaking gently to patients and checking dosages with practiced care, yet beneath that steadiness there is a constant expectation that something terrible could happen again at any moment.
